query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of a ductile phase-forming element like Cu to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy will increase its load-bearing integrity by 15% while preserving its caloric performance under applied-field and pressure-field operation.
generation.intervention: adding a small amount of Cu

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the load-bearing integrity does not increase by at least 10% or the caloric performance decreases by more than 5%, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Equiatomic multi-component metallic materials, referred to variously as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), multi-component alloys or compositionally complex alloys, have generated considerable excitement in the materials science community of late as a new class of materials that derive their properties not from a single dominant constituent, such as iron in steels, but rather from multiple principal elements with the potential for unique combinations of mechanical properties compared with conventional alloys. Much of the interest is predicated on the belief that many new alloys with useful properties are likely to be discovered near the centres (as opposed to the corners) of phase diagrams in compositionally complex systems. One of the extensively investigated high-entropy alloys, an equiatomic, face-centred cubic (fcc) metallic alloy comprising five transition elements, Cr, Mn Fe, Co and Ni, was introduced in 2004 (ref. ), although it was not for a decade that its mechanical properties were first systematically characterized. Strength and ductility (and hence toughness) are key mechanical properties of structural materials, although these properties are often mutually exclusive. In crystalline metallic materials, strength and ductility depend on the presence of crystal defects and how they move under mechanical loading. Dislocations serve as the prime carrier of plasticity in metals and their motion to create plastic deformation is strongly influenced by interactions with other dislocations as well as defects such as solute atoms, stacking faults, grain boundaries (GBs) and reinforcement particles or precipitates. In general, strong interactions (obstacles) strengthen a material although this often limits its ability to plastically deform. Twinning, however, appears to be a deformation mechanism capable of defeating this ‘conflict' between strength and ductility. The presence of twins usually serves to impede dislocation motion and induce strengthening, but multiple twinning systems can also enhance ductility.
